candidates.topic: Humans produce enough saliva to fill two swimming pools in a lifetime
candidates.teaser: Your mouth is hiding a secret that'll make you rethink everything you sip today.
candidates.video_title: Your Body Does This Every Single Day (You Had No Idea)
candidates.video_description: Over a lifetime, the human body produces an almost unbelievable amount of saliva. It's not just for digestion — saliva is one of the most complex fluids your body makes. The numbers will genuinely shock you.
candidates.script: Your body is doing something right now that you completely ignore — and it has been doing it every single second since you were born. Over the course of your lifetime, your mouth produces enough saliva to fill not one, but two full-sized swimming pools. That's over 25,000 liters of liquid, packed with enzymes, proteins, and antimicrobial agents powerful enough to start breaking down food before you even swallow. Saliva actually kills bacteria, helps wounds in your mouth heal faster than anywhere else on your body, and without it, you literally could not taste anything. So here's what I want to know — does knowing this make you more impressed by your body, or just a little grossed out?

candidates.topic: The Eiffel Tower has a rival that was almost built in Barcelona
candidates.teaser: Paris almost didn't get the Eiffel Tower — another city had first dibs and said no.
candidates.video_title: Paris Almost Didn't Get the Eiffel Tower
candidates.video_description: Gustave Eiffel originally pitched his iconic iron tower to Barcelona, not Paris. The city rejected it completely, calling it an eyesore. Paris only got the tower because they were desperate for a centerpiece for the 1889 World's Fair.
candidates.script: The Eiffel Tower is the ultimate symbol of Paris — but Paris was never actually the first choice. Gustave Eiffel originally pitched his revolutionary iron structure to the city of Barcelona for their 1888 World's Fair. The city's officials took one look at the design and flat-out rejected it, calling it industrial, ugly, and completely out of place. So Eiffel turned around, walked straight to Paris, and offered it for the 1889 World's Fair instead. At first, hundreds of Parisian artists signed a petition calling it a metal monstrosity. Today, it's the most visited paid monument on the entire planet. So the real question is — what would Barcelona look like right now if they had just said yes?

candidates.topic: Cuttlefish can see polarized light and are colorblind yet perfectly camouflage
candidates.teaser: This sea creature is completely colorblind — yet its camouflage is so perfect it seems impossible.
candidates.video_title: This Animal Is Colorblind But Has Perfect Camouflage
candidates.video_description: Cuttlefish are masters of disguise, able to mimic textures, patterns, and colors in milliseconds. The twist? They are completely colorblind. Scientists still don't fully understand how they pull it off.
candidates.script: Imagine being completely colorblind — unable to see a single shade of red, blue, or green — yet being the greatest master of color disguise on the entire planet. That's the cuttlefish. This bizarre sea creature can change its skin color, texture, and pattern in under one second to perfectly match its surroundings. It can mimic sand, coral, even the shadows of moving waves. But here's the part that baffles scientists: cuttlefish have only one type of color receptor in their eyes, meaning they technically see the world in black and white. One leading theory is that they use the shape of their pupils to detect polarized light and decode color that way — a form of vision no human has ever experienced. So how exactly does a colorblind animal outsmart every predator using color? Science still doesn't have a complete answer.

candidates.topic: Ancient Romans used crushed mouse brains as toothpaste
candidates.teaser: What ancient Romans put in their mouths every morning will genuinely disturb you.
candidates.video_title: What Romans Used as Toothpaste Will Disgust You
candidates.video_description: Ancient Romans had surprisingly advanced dental hygiene routines — but the ingredients they used were absolutely horrifying by modern standards. From crushed bones to mouse brains, their toothpaste recipes are a wild window into the ancient world.
candidates.script: Every morning, ancient Romans brushed their teeth — which sounds surprisingly civilized until you find out what they used. Roman toothpaste recipes included powdered animal bones, oyster shells, charcoal, and in some documented formulas, crushed mouse brains. They also rinsed with human urine, which was actually collected and sold specifically for teeth whitening because of its ammonia content. And here's the disturbing twist — it kind of worked. Studies on Roman skeletons have shown that their teeth were often in better condition than people living in the 18th century, centuries later. So the Romans were onto something, even if the method was absolutely revolting. Would you try it if it actually guaranteed perfect teeth?

candidates.topic: There is a place on Earth where two oceans meet but don't mix
candidates.teaser: Two of Earth's oceans crash into each other every single day — and refuse to mix.
candidates.video_title: Two Oceans Meet Here But Never Mix. Here's Why.
candidates.video_description: At the southern tip of Africa, the Atlantic and Indian Oceans collide in a stunning visible line on the water's surface. Despite being side by side, their waters maintain distinct temperatures, salinity levels, and even colors. The science behind it is fascinating.
candidates.script: At the very southern tip of Africa, something happens that looks like it belongs in a movie. The Atlantic Ocean and the Indian Ocean crash into each other — and you can actually see the line where they meet. The water on each side is a different color, a different temperature, and a different texture. But despite constantly colliding, they refuse to mix. The reason comes down to physics: the two oceans have dramatically different salt concentrations and densities, creating what scientists call a halocline — essentially an invisible wall of water pressure that keeps them separated. The same phenomenon happens where rivers meet the sea, and the line can persist for miles. It's one of the most visually stunning things on Earth, and most people have never even heard of it. What other boundaries like this do you think are hiding on this planet?
